questions.prompt: When the model matches the plant and both are driven by the same \(u\), the estimation error \(\tilde{x} = x - \hat{x}\) obeys
questions.explanation: The plant and the model share \(A\), \(B\), and \(u\), so those terms cancel in \(x - \hat{x}\). What remains is the correction \(L\) times the output residual, which produces \(A - LC\). The state-feedback matrix \(A - BK\) is a different design. Dropping \(A\), or calling the measurement itself the error, describes a different equation.

questions.prompt: The scalar plant is \(\dot{x} = -2x\), \(y = 4x\). The observer gain that places the error eigenvalue at \(-9\) is
questions.explanation: \(-2 - 4L = -9\) gives \(4L = 7\), so \(L = 1.75\). Using \(L = 9/4 = 2.25\) forgets that the output is already scaled by 4 and lands at \(-2 - 9 = -11\). Solving \(-2 - 4L = 0\), which only moves the pole to the origin, gives \(L = -0.5\). Forgetting the output scale and solving \(-2 - L = -9\) produces 7, the gap rather than the gain.

questions.prompt: The desired error poles are \(-6\) and \(-10\). In the monic polynomial \((s+6)(s+10)\), the coefficient of \(s\) is
questions.explanation: \((s+6)(s+10) = s^2 + 16s + 60\). The coefficient of \(s\) is 16, the sum of the pole magnitudes. The product 60 is the constant term. The gap \(10 - 6 = 4\) is not a coefficient. Using only the faster pole, 10, drops the other one.

questions.prompt: A scalar plant is \(\dot{x} = a x\), \(y = c x\), and the observer gain is g. Write the eigenvalue of the estimation-error system in the names a, c, and g.
questions.explanation: The error pole is \(a - g c\). The product \(gc\) is the correction, and \(a\) is still the open-loop coefficient. \(a + gc\) is the sign you get by subtracting the residual in the wrong direction. \(a - g\) drops the output scale \(c\).

questions.prompt: Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -4 & -3 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(C = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\). The desired error polynomial is \(s^2 + 12s + 32\). The gain entry that multiplies the residual into the first state is
questions.explanation: With \(L = \begin{bmatrix} l_1 \\ l_2 \end{bmatrix}\), \(A - LC = \begin{bmatrix} -l_1 & 1 \\ -4 - l_2 & -3 \end{bmatrix}\). The coefficient of \(s\) is \(l_1 + 3\), so \(l_1 = 9\). The constant term \(3 l_1 + l_2 + 4\) then fixes \(l_2 = 1\), the other entry. Reporting 12 returns the desired coefficient before the open-loop 3 is removed. Reporting 3 returns that open-loop piece alone.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>an output row that reads the first state</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">1   0</text></svg>

questions.prompt: Put these observer-design steps in the order you would do them.
questions.explanation: Observability is what makes an arbitrary error polynomial attainable, so it comes first. The speed relative to the control poles is a design choice you write down before the algebra. Matching coefficients is the solve. The last check is both algebraic and practical: a correct polynomial can still amplify noise if the gain is huge.

steps: Confirm that the observability matrix has full rank.
Choose error poles faster than the state-feedback poles already placed, and write their monic polynomial.
Write the characteristic polynomial of A - LC with the gain entries unknown.
Match coefficients and solve for L.
Check the eigenvalues of A - LC, and check that L is not so large that sensor noise dominates the correction.

questions.prompt: The output is \(y = Cx\), the observability matrix has full rank, and the same \(u\) drives the plant and the model. One step is wrong.
questions.explanation: The error matrix is \(A - LC\). State feedback builds \(A - BK\) from the input matrix, and that gain does not appear in the error equation when the model matches. The residual update, the rank hypothesis, and the decay of a stable error system are the right pieces.

steps: The estimate is corrected by \(L\) times the residual \(y - C\hat{x}\).
Full rank means the eigenvalues of the error system can be assigned.
The estimation-error matrix is \(A - BK\), the matrix state feedback uses.
When the model matches, a stable \(A - LC\) drives the estimation error to zero.
reasons: The error matrix is A - LC, built from the output row, not A - BK.
Full rank of the observability matrix means the error is already zero.
The residual should be added with no gain at all.

questions.prompt: A usual reason to place the observer poles faster than the state-feedback poles is that
questions.explanation: The control law was derived as \(u = -Kx\). While \(\hat{x}\) is still far from \(x\), that law is being fed the wrong vector. A faster error transient shortens that interval. It does not cancel zeros, it does not force the two matrices to be equal, and a faster pole makes \(L\) larger, not zero.

the estimate settles before a law designed for a known state has to act for long on a bad estimate

questions.prompt: Which statements hold for a linear observer?
questions.explanation: Observability is the dual of reachability, so a full-rank pair can assign every error eigenvalue. An incorrect \(B\) leaves a term in \(u\) inside the error equation, which is why the model has to see the same command the plant sees. A larger \(L\) amplifies sensor noise. And the copy of the plant is \(\dot{\hat{x}} = A\hat{x} + Bu + L(y - C\hat{x})\), so a nonzero \(B\) makes \(u\) part of the update.

options: If \((A, C)\) is observable, every eigenvalue of \(A - LC\) can be assigned.
If the model uses the wrong \(B\), the input \(u\) still drives the estimation error.
A larger \(L\) always reduces the effect of sensor noise on the estimate.
When \(B\) is not zero, the observer equation needs \(u\) as well as \(y\).

questions.prompt: Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -6 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(C = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\). The desired error polynomial is \(s^2 + 12s + 35\). The gain entry that multiplies the residual into the second state is
questions.explanation: \(A - LC = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 - l_1 \\ -6 & -1 - l_2 \end{bmatrix}\). The coefficient of \(s\) is \(1 + l_2\), so \(l_2 = 11\). The constant term \(6 - 6 l_1\) fixes the other entry, \(l_1 = -29/6\), which is not this question. Adding the desired coefficient to the open-loop 1, getting 13, counts that 1 twice. Using the constant term 35 as a gain ignores the open-loop \(-6\).

questions.prompt: State feedback \(u = -K\hat{x}\) is built from this estimate. The eigenvalues of the combined loop are
questions.explanation: When the model matches, a coordinate change splits the closed loop into the state-feedback block and the error block. The spectrum is the union of the two spectra you placed. Either block alone is only half of that spectrum, and the open-loop \(A\) is what you moved away from.

questions.explanation: Both designs correct a model with a gain times the output residual. Here the numbers in \(L\) come from a polynomial you chose. The later design computes those numbers from the two noise intensities, and that calculation is not the same as an arbitrary pole list. The error system stays linear for a linear plant. The output is still the signal the correction uses.
